observation: Inference providers must keep many LLMs available, including low-volume but essential models, while token prices fall, making resource efficiency increasingly important. To meet strict SLOs they dedicate GPU groups per model, yet production GPU duty cycles commonly fall below 30%. Analyses of production traces from major inference providers (Hyperbolic, Novita AI) and Chatbot Arena reveal a dynamic, rapidly shifting bursty-group pattern: requests concentrate on a small subset of concurrently active models and that subset changes frequently (23%–50% of models active on average; active set changes 54–766 times per hour), and per-model request streams are extremely volatile with abrupt pattern shifts and many idle intervals. In such conditions pure time sharing causes repeated model swapping, thrashing, and SLO-violating queuing spikes, while pure space sharing leaves memory locked to idle models (in the Novita AI trace models are idle over 70% of the time and roughly 50% of GPU memory is occupied but unused), starving active models during bursts. Thus neither sharing strategy alone can satisfy SLOs and efficiency under realistic multi-LLM workloads; what is needed is a fluid combination of both.

solution.idea: The prior work advances execution within a single loaded model, but none of it decides which complete LLMs should be resident in GPU memory at any moment. Orca-style iteration-level batching and vLLM-style paged KV caches assume the model's weights are already pinned; AlpaServe's model sharding enables statistical multiplexing, but its placement is computed offline from profiled rates, so abrupt shifts in the active model set are exactly what it cannot absorb; disaggregated prefill/decode systems schedule phases of one or a few high-rate workloads and leave dormant full-size models occupying memory; S-LoRA and Punica page only tiny adapter deltas, not full LLM weights. Pure time sharing fails because every new burst forces a model swap that queues requests behind loading; pure space sharing fails because an idle model keeps its memory reservation while an active model starves. The key missing piece is a fluid residency controller that makes GPU memory a working set of full models and makes GPU execution an iteration-level time-shared resource shared by that working set. I therefore propose a two-timescale serving control plane. At a slow, configurable interval, a model-residency planner computes which full models should be space-shared into GPU memory for the next interval, using a short-term demand forecast, per-model SLO weight, memory footprint, and transition cost. At a fast, iteration-level timescale, an Orca-style continuous scheduler batches tokens from every currently resident model onto the same GPU workers without swapping weights, so a model that is resident never suffers a load stall. The fluidity comes from an explicit transition mechanism: when the active set begins to change, the planner promotes the incoming model and demotes an outgoing idle model in overlapping make-before-break steps, using a small memory reserve and hysteresis thresholds. This replaces the binary choice of whether to time-share or space-share with the control question of how many models to hold resident and how long to hold them after their burst. The alternatives I considered and rejected were: pure LRU weight paging, which thrashes under frequent active-set changes; keeping every model resident, which wastes the observed 50% of GPU memory occupied by idle models; and a static AlpaServe placement, which cannot adapt to shifts. The direction is justified by the trace pattern: only a minority of models are active at once, so the resident working set can be small enough to fit in GPU memory, and the active-set changes are infrequent relative to iteration execution, so overlapping transitions can hide most model loading overhead.
solution.implementation: The system is implemented as a cluster-level control plane above a pool of GPU workers, a high-bandwidth model store (NVMe/DRAM) holding all model weights, and a distributed iteration scheduler. Each model m has a GPU parameter footprint w_m, a predicted arrival rate a_m, an SLO priority p_m, an approximate load time s_m, and a quiescence timer. GPU memory is not statically partitioned; each worker exposes a memory allocator that can pin or release whole model weight pages. The control plane runs in epochs of length E (default a few seconds, an order of magnitude smaller than typical model-load time). At each epoch it performs the following: (1) Monitoring: accumulate per-model request counts and queue lengths, and maintain a short-window EWMA and a long-window EWMA of arrival rates. A model is flagged as a change candidate if its short-window rate exceeds the long-window rate by a factor, or if it has queued requests while not resident. (2) Forecasting: for each model, estimate the expected number of arrivals in the next horizon H, where H is at least one model-load time; the forecast is used only to decide residency, not to predict exact token counts. (3) Residency planning: every epoch, the planner computes a target resident set R. A model is always placed in R if it has active requests or if its expected arrivals in H exceed a promote threshold. The planner greedily adds candidate models in decreasing order of p_m * expected arrivals / w_m, and keeps a memory reserve of a fixed fraction (e.g., 10%) of aggregate GPU memory for transition overlap. If R exceeds available memory, it first removes models whose quiescence timer has elapsed and that have no active requests; if none are removable, it does not promote a lower-priority model, and new requests for that model wait in a bounded queue until a slot frees. To prevent thrashing, promotion and demotion use hysteresis: a model is demoted only after it has had no requests for T_idle epochs, and promotion is cancelled if the model becomes idle before its load completes. (4) Transition protocol: to promote model m, the planner issues a background load of m's weight pages from the model store into spare GPU memory, overlapping with execution of currently resident models; when the last page arrives, m is enabled and its queued requests are inserted as new iteration sequences. To demote an idle model, the planner first marks it retiring, allows its in-flight requests to drain, then moves its KV pages to the eviction pool and releases its weight pages in reverse order of expected future use. Promotion and demotion are overlapped: a model being promoted uses only the reserved memory slack, so it does not force termination of active work. (5) Execution scheduling: on each GPU worker, the iteration scheduler continuously forms micro-batches from all enabled resident models. It maintains separate paged KV caches per model, as in vLLM, but model parameters remain pinned only while the model is in R. Tokens from different resident models are interleaved at the granularity of decoder iterations using a weighted earliest-deadline order; a model with no queued work consumes no execution time. This is the time-sharing dimension, while residency in R is the space-sharing dimension. The system resolves bursts by relying on iteration-level batching inside any resident model: once a model is resident, even a sudden dense burst is absorbed by the scheduler without model swapping. When a completely non-resident model receives an unexpected burst, the planner immediately starts promotion; if no memory slack is available, it demotes the lowest-priority resident model that has no active requests, under the same make-before-break protocol. For essential low-volume models that must never suffer cold-start delay, the planner can assign a minimum residency quota, but only up to a small fraction of total memory, and it always monitors whether that quota is actually being used. All parameters of the controller—the epoch length E, forecast horizon H, idle timeout T_idle, promote/demote thresholds, and memory reserve fraction—are configurable, allowing the operator to trade responsiveness against memory efficiency. The design relies on no measurement claim; its feasibility follows from the observations that active-set shifts are frequent enough to need planning but not faster than the scheduler epoch, and that at any time the active working set is small enough to be resident, while the previously idle models can provide the reclaimable memory needed to stage the next active set.
